archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: War coming: Italy alerted.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “There was no danger in now allowing the viceroy to return, as he was sincerely attached to his wife. In a letter of the 17th August, Napoleon wrote thus to his brother Joseph — " I should much like to see a revolt on the part of the canaille of Naples. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Prince Eugene from 14M, 1806-08-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — I thank you for what you say about my fete day. Affairs are getting settled. I will soon send you instructions for your voyage to Paris. I know that you wish to come here. You will see the Queen of Holland. We will keep the princess until after her confinement. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Italy braced for war.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Daughter, — I have read with pleasure your letter of the loth. You are right to rely upon my affection. Take care of yourself in your present condition, and try and not give us a daughter. I would give you a recipe for that, but you would not believe in it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Bavarian alliance flattered.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" Bamberg, Uh October, 1 806. " Soldiers! — Orders for your return to France had been issued. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Marshal Berthier from T-7Th, 1806-09-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with surprise that the chief of the staff dares to correspond with the enemy without your permission. General Caesar Berthier is then ignorant of his duty! The reply of Sidney Smith is impertinent, as is everything which emanates from that officer. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, St.  Cloud, 1806-09-07
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Hold Naples while Prussia falls.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I must wait therefore for some days to see what will happen. Send some Polish officers to the Russian frontier to see what is going on. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Marshal Berthier from St. Cloud, 1806-09-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see no inconvenience in granting Marshal Ney leave for twenty days to be present at the confinement of his wife. You can also give a similar leave on the same conditions, and under the same pretext, to Marshal Davoust, should he wish to take advantage of it.,. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Marshal Berthier from St; Cloud, 1806-09-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have recognised him as a prince, and have given him the grand cordon of the Legion of Honour. As I shall be obliged to consult the people with regard to his right of succession to the throne, I hope that Lucien will not allow this opportunity to escape. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Holland, St.  Cloud, 1806-09-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Holland from St. Cloud, 1806-09-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Mr. Fox is dying. Lord Yarmouth has been received in London in triumph because he was known to belong to the peace party. The illness of Mr. Fox has filled the nation with consternation. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Naples, St.  Cloud, 1806-09-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Naples from St. Cloud, 1806-09-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I was just going to send you orders for the return of the army, when I learned that the Emperor of Russia had refused to ratify the treaty. I must wait therefore for some days to see what will happen. Send some Polish officers to the Russian frontier to see what is going on. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: The army gathers for Prussia.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You have heard of the armaments made by Prussia, and the non-ratification of Russia. My negotiations with ' England are not broken off, but they put forward the most extraordinary pretensions. They wish to have Surinam, Berbice, and all your colonies. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Holland, St.  Cloud, 1806-09-10
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Louis: guard the coasts.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Good Friend, — My affairs are going on as well as I hoped. With the aid of God they will, I think, have assumed a terrible character for the poor King of Prussia, whom I pity personally, for he is a good man. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Gera, 1806-10-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Although we were in their country, they appeared quite ignorant of our movements. The Emperor visited the field of Rosbach, and ordered the column which had been erected there to be sent to Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Clarke from Weimar, 1806-10-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I convinced her that her husband was guilty, and that, according to the laws of war, he ought to be executed. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Princess Ferdinand Of Prussia, BERLIN)  iZth, 1806-10-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Princess Ferdinand Of Prussia from Berlin) Izth, 1806-10-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the letter of your Royal Highness. I was much touched by the position of Madame de Hatzfeld. I convinced her that her husband was guilty, and that, according to the laws of war, he ought to be executed. However, I spared him even the disagreeableness of a trial. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: From occupied Berlin: courtesy to the defeated dynasty.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Lord Morpeth, sent by the court of London to deal in Prussian blood, mission unworthy of a man like him, reached Weimar on the nth with seductive offers and offers of large subsidies. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. De Talleyrand from Dessau, 1806-10-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Immediately after the battle of Jena the King of Prussia sent me an aide-de-camp with a letter. To-day he sends me the Marquis de Lucchesini. I have ordered. him to remain at the outposts, and I have sent Duroc to know what he wants. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Jena won: diplomacy follows cannon.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Captive Officers after the Battle of/e/ia, Oct. 75, 1806. " I know not why I am at war with your sovereign. He is a wise, pacific prince, deserving of respect. I wisli to see your country rescued from its humiliating dependence upon Prussia. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Magnanimity after Jena.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I have manoeuvred finely against the Prussians. Yesterday I gained a great victory. They had 150,000 men. I took 30,000 prisoners, lOO guns and standards. I was in presence and close to the King of Prussia; I nearly captured him and the queen. I have been bivouacking for two days. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Jena eve: writing Josephine before the battle.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received many letters from you. I can write you but a word. My affairs are very prosperous. I shall be tomorrow at Potsdam, and the 25th at Berlin. I am remarkably well; fatigue refreshes me. I am very happy to hear that you are with Hortense and Stephanie, in very good company. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Wittenberg: prosperous affairs, off to Potsdam.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “". You are the worthy defenders of my crown and of the glory of this grand nation. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Naples from 25M, 1806-10-25. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have crushed the Prussian monarchy; I shall crush the Russians if they arrive. I no longer fear the. Austrians. I shall not ask you for any troops; I have no need of them. If, however, you could send me sOme cavalry, do so." We have two letters written from Potsdam on the subject of the theatre. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Berlin's fall announced to Joseph.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They implored Napoleon not to sully his own glory, and to make his comrades executiorlers. The Emperor remained inflexible, and if the Prince had not been concealed for a time by Savage and Caulaincourt, he would certainly have been shot. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Berlin, 1806-11-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 26th of October. We have here superb weather. You will see by the bulletin that we have taken Stellin.* It is a very strong place. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Berlin: superb weather, bulletins tell the rest.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your Highness says in your letter that you were obliged to wage war against me; you will not find it ill therefore that I should wish to have at Fulde a prince who is master to remain at peace with me. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Prince Of Orange from 8M, 1806-11-08. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am sorry to think that you do not anluse yourself at Mayence. ' If the voyage were not so long you might come here, for there are no more enemies this side of the Vistula. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Berlin, 1806-11-16. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am at Kustrin in order to make some reconnaissances. I shall see, in two days, if you can come. Hold yourself in readiness. I hope that the Queen of Holland will be of the party. It is two o'clock in the morning. I have just risen; this is the custom of war. "NAPOLEON.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Pursuit into Poland.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am going to take a town in Poland. This is the first town. This evening I shall be at Posen. After that I will call you to Berlin, so that we may arrive there on the same day. My health is good. The weather is rather bad; it has been raining for three days. My affairs are going on well. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Poland: mud, cold, billets.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “This enthusiasm was, as Napoleon admitted the next day in a letter to Murat, somewhat circumspect. Murat thought. that he was going to reign at Warsaw, and so did Prince Jerome, but it was not the intention of Napoleon for the moment to break with Austria. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Cambaceres from Posen, 1806-12-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “This is most important, as it is absolutely necessary to isolate England. A similar letter was written to Prince Eugene with regard to " my kingdom of Italy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Gaudin from Posen, 1806-12-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" March upon Choczim; you have nothing to fear from Russia. " I have directed my ambassador (Sebastiani) to contract the necessary engagements with you. If you have been too prudent up to the present, a longer condescendence towards Russia would be a weakness which would ruin your empire. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Sultan Selim from Posen, 1806-12-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Have a circular written, and take measures so that, throughout the extent of the empire, all letters coming from England, or written in English and by Englishmen, be seized. This is most important, as it is absolutely necessary to isolate England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Finances follow the eagles into Poland.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Prussia, which had formed a league with Russia, has disappeared. I have destroyed her armies, and am master of her strong places. " My armies are upon the Vistula, and Warsaw is in my power. "Prussian and Russian Poland are rising, and are forming armies to reconquer their independence. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: The eastern alliance: Paris courts Constantinople.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “To-day is the anniversary of Austerlitz. I have been to a ball given by the city. It rains. I am well. I love you, and long for you. My troops are at Warsaw. It is not yet cold. All the Polish ladies are French, but there is only one woman for me. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Posen, Austerlitz anniversary: ball, rain, love.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I write a line only, my friend. I am in a wretched barn. I have beaten the Russians. I have captured thirty guns, their baggage, and 6,000 men. The weather is fearful; it rains, and we have mud up to the knee. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Golymin, 1806-12-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “However, I should see you return to Paris, where you are desired, with pleasure. You know that I depend upon events. All my affairs are going on well. Adieu, my friend. I have made peace with Saxony. "NAPOLEON. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Posen, 1806-12-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I am starting for Warsaw. I shall be back in a fortnight, when I hope I shall be able to send for you. However, I should see you return to Paris, where you are desired, with pleasure. You know that I depend upon events. All my affairs are going on well. Adieu, my friend. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Posen winter: love amid snow.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I leave immediately for Warsaw. In a fortnight I shall be on my return. I hope that then I shall be able to send for you. Nevertheless, should there be still delay, I should see you with pleasure return to Paris, where you are desired. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Posen: off to Warsaw, back in a fortnight.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received no news from you, my love. I am very well. I have been at Warsaw for two days. My affairs go on well. The weather is very mild, and even a little humid. We have as yet had scarcely any frost. It is the weather of October. Adieu, my love. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Warsaw two days: affairs go well.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I can write you but a word, my love. I am in a wretched barn. I have beaten the Russians. I have taken thirty pieces of cannon, their baggage, and have made six thousand prisoners. But the weather is frightful. It rains; we have mud to the knees. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Golymin barn: beaten Russians, thirty guns.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “THE YEAR 1807. The principal events of the year 1807 were the battles of Eylau and Friedland, which were followed by the treaty of Tilsit, the invasion of Portugal, and preparations for the invasion of Spain; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Pultusk, 1806-12-31. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I laughed heartily on receiving your last letter. You have formed an idea of the belles of Poland which they do not deserve. I received your letter in a wretched. barn, having mud, wind, and straw for my bed {sic). To-morrow I shall be at Warsaw. I think that everything is finished for this year. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Winter war: Pultusk's bloody snow.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Entering Warsaw, Jan. z, 1801. " Soldiers: It is a year this very hour since you were on the field of Austerlitz, where the Russian battalions fled in disorder, or surrendered up their arms to their conquerors. Next day proposals of peace were talked of, but they were deceptive. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Warsaw proclamation.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" The Emperor complains that he receives nothing new from Paris. It would be easy for you to forward two or three volumes every day by the courier which leaves at 8 A.M. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Marshal Berthier from Warsaw, 1807-01-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “According to the French returns it was afterwards shown that during this short campaign no less than 420,000 men were received into hospital, 210,000 fever patients, and 100,000 wounded men, and that 32,000 men died. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Izth, 1807-01-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother, — I congratulate myself on the peace which unites us, and which time will only strengthen. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Saxony, Warsaw, 1807-01-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Saxony from Warsaw, 1807-01-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — I beg that you will spare the states of Mecklenberg Strelitz. There is a grandmother of the Princesse Eugene there. She is an old woman; see if she wants anything, and inform her that you have been ordered to treat her with particular attention. " Napoleon.". To M. RISSAULT, Librarian. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Winter quarters staff work.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You must allow the Place de la Concorde to retain its present name. Concorde, this is what renders France invincible. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Interior from Poland.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" My Cousin, — Write to my minister at Dresden so that the Saxon contingent may arrive as soon as possible at Glogau. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Naples from 2Zth, 1807-01-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think that you have done wrong to create marshals, which has the inconvenience of costing money, and of giving men who have done little great pretensions. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Holland, Warsaw, 1807-01-02
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Louis ordered across winter Poland.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I am deeply afiected by all that you say to me; but the season cold, the roads wretched, the region unsafe, I can not consent to expose you to such perils and dangers. Return to Paris, to pass the winter there. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Warsaw cold, roads wretched, region unsafe.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" Napoleon. " All the great officers of the state were supposed to spend money in entertaining so as* to keep Paris gay. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Lebrun from 7S)Th, 1807-01-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 17th, and thank you for all you say. I am aware of your attachment, which I greatly prize. What are you doing in Paris } I have not heard that you gave a little ball during the Carnival. " Napoleon. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Paris governed from Warsaw snow.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “« Napoleon " In fact some 10,000 Hessians refused for a time to lay down their arms. On the same day his Majesty wrote to the King of Holland complaining that according to reports from London trade "with Holland was just as brisk as before the decree of Berlin. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Cambacfires from Warsaw, 1807-01-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

sourceTitle: To The King Of Naples, Warsaw, 1807-01-14
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Naples from Warsaw, 1807-01-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Turkey has declared war against Russia. A Tartar who left Constantinople on the 2nd brings me excellent news from that country. " A million has been forwarded to you from Turin. My health never was better, and the consequence is that I have become more galant than formerly. " Napoleon.”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, Warsaw, 1807-01-14
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Joseph summoned east in thought.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 3 ist December. The affair of Hesse Cassel is terminated. It appears that it was the soldiery which wished to move. « Napoleon " In fact some 10,000 Hessians refused for a time to lay down their arms. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Arch-chancellor instructed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “• No doubt an invisible power, the same which caused me to conquer, and which watches over your glory, wished to drag our enemies to their destruction in blindly arming them against the forces of three powerful empires. Let us all three join together and form an eternal alliance. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Warsaw, 1807-01-16. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My good Friend, — I have received your letter of the 5th; what you say of your grief gives me pain. Why these tears, this chagrin.' I shall soon see you; do not doubt my sentiments; and if you wish to be still dearer to me exhibit greater strength of mind. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Warsaw separation lengthens.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I fear that you are greatly disappointed in view of our separation, which must yet be prolonged some weeks, and of your return to Paris. I expect of you more force of character. They tell me that you weep continually. Fi! how unbecoming that is. Your letter of the 7th of January gave me much pain. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Warsaw: separation prolonged, return deferred.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I am in the receipt of your letter. I have smiled at your fear for my safety. I am in despair at the tone of your letters, and at what I hear of you. I forbid you to weep, to be melancholy and anxious; I wish that you may be cheerful, amiable, and happy. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Smiled at her fears; despair at her tone.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I thought in my ignorance that the wife was made for the husband, the husband for the country, his family, and glory; forgive my error, one has always something to learn from you pretty women " NAPOLEON.". […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Warsaw, 1807-01-21. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter of the llth, from Mayence, made me smile. I am, to-day, one hundred and twenty miles from Warsaw. The weather is cold but fine. Adieu, my love; be happy; have character. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: 120 miles from Warsaw; cold weather.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “period to the misfortunes of your family, and to organize, as speedily as possible, the Prussian monarchy. Its intermediate power is necessary for the tranquillity of Europe. I desire peace with Russia; and, provided the Cabinet of St Petersburg has no designs upon the Turkish Empire, I see no difficulty in obtaining it. […]”
sourceTitle: Letter to the King of Prussia, 1807-02-01
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Peace offered to Prussia after Eylau; month certain.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is 2 A.M. I am tired. I can write only a few words. Marshal Duroc will inform you that I gained a victory yesterday over the Russian army. " As for the communication made by the King of Prussia, I think that you may reply to this effect: […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. De Talleyrand from Eylau, 1807-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I fought a battle yesterday and gained the victory, but I lost a great many men. However, you will find the details in the bulletin, which is exact. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Cambacires from Eylau, 1807-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Believe me that this will be the happiest moment of my life; I flatter myself that it will be the commencement of a durable friendship between us. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Prussia, I'^th, 1807-02-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Prussia from I'^Th, 1807-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Lestocg took the enemy in flank and decided the victory in favour of the Russians. The Russians lost 20,000 men killed and wounded. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Eylau, 1807-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Our affairs here could not be going on better. A corps of 20,000 men has beep cut off. The Russian army is flying it knows not where, in the greatest disorder; artillery baggage, magazines are falling into our hands. My only fear is lest the corps cut off should be Prussian corps. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Eylau eve diplomacy.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother, — I send you my aide-de-camp, General Bertrand, who possesses my entire confidence. He has things to say to you which I hope will prove agreeable. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Prussia, I'^th, 1807-02-01
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Peace offered to a beaten king.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The loss of the enemy, which is still more considerable, does not console me. I write these few lines to you myself, although I am very tired, to tell you that I am well and that I love you. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Eylau, 1807-02-03. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In consequence of the bad weather I shall go into cantonments. " I beg of you not to be disconsolate; all this will soon be finished, and the happiness of seeing you will make me promptly forget my fatigues. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Eylau, 1807-02-03. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — There was a great battle yesterday; I gained the victory, but we have lost a great many men. The loss of the enemy, which is still more considerable, does not console me. I write these few lines to you myself, although I am very tired, to tell you that I am well and that I love you. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Eylau: victory remains, at cost.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — I am in pursuit of the Russian army. I have driven it from all its positions, and am going to force it back behind the Niemen. It is splendid weather, and everything is going on well. « NAPOLEON.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Paris after Eylau's butchery.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — there was a great battle yesterday. Victory remains with me, but I have lost many men. The loss of the enemy, still more considerable, does not console me. I write these few lines myself, though greatly fatigued, to tell you that I am well, and that I love you. Wholly thine. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Eylau, day after: victory remains, many men lost.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “he suffered horridly. I have lost 1,600 killed and between 3,000 and 4,000 wounded. "Napoleon." ' Similar letters were written in various directions, and the Russian loss was set down at 30,000 men. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from 9M, 1807-02-09. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you one line, my love. You must have been very anxious. I have beaten the enemy in a memorable battle, but it has cost me many brave men. The inclement weather constrains me to return to my cantonments. Do not indulge in grief, I entreat you. All this will soon end. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Eylau: memorable battle, at cost.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you a letter from General Darmagnac; he is a very good soldier, who commanded the thirty-second. He is much attached to me. If this Madame de Richemont is rich, and it would be a good match, I should see the marriage with pleasure. Introduce them to each other. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Darmagnac's letter forwarded; a good soldier.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I am still at Eylau. The country is covered with the dead and the wounded. This is not the pleasant part of war. One suffers, and the soul is oppressed to see so many victims. I am well. I have done what I wished. I have repulsed the enemy, compelling him to abandon his projects. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Still at Eylau: dead and wounded as far as eyes see.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I write you two words. I am very well. I am in movement to put my army into winter quarters. It rains and thaws as in the month of April. We have not yet had one cold day. Adieu, my love. Entirely thine. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Moving to winter quarters; rain and thaw.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am informed that the commerce between England and Holland was never more brisk than since the Berlin. decree, and the communications with England more rapid and more numerous. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Fouche from Llebstadt, 1807-02-20. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Spread the following reports in an official manner. They are, however, true. Spread them first in the salons and then put them in the papers — that the Russian army is greatly weakened, that some regiments are reduced to 150 men. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Paris police from snowy Osterode.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The partisan SchiU has been cut off from Kolberg. That wretch, who is a sort of brigand, has fallen back on 1 Koeslin. Send some Saxon or Polish cavalry in pursuit of this wretch. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Danzig must fall: siege orders.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “As for the officers asked for, it will be necessary to know the number required, their rank, and branch. I sent you a letter yesterday for Marshal Massena, who I suppose has joined his army corps. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. De Talleyrand from Osterode, 1807-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am now told that there were only from 4,000 to 4,500 men wounded." And — "All this is a tissue of lies. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Naples, OSTERODE, 1807-03-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Naples from Osterode, 1807-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The French ambassador, Andreossy, was to say that independently of the 140,000 men which the Emperor had in his depots in France, he had just raised 80,000 conscripts of the class of 1808; that in addition he had created ten legions of reserve, each composed of five battalions; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Fouche from Osterode, 1807-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — Your letter grieves me. You are not going to die, you are in good health, and have no reason for sorrow. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Osterode, 1807-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Since the Porte refuses to have troops at Constantinople or in Bosnia, you can assure the ambassador that it shall no longer be a question of this. As for the officers asked for, it will be necessary to know the number required, their rank, and branch. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Spring diplomacy from Osterode.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 20th. The Enghsh squadron is before Constantinople. I have received news up to the loth February, which shows that the English ambassador has left Constantinople. We shall now see how all this will end. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, OSTERODE, 1807-03-01
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Joseph reminded from the snow.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — it is two or three days since I have written to you. I reproach myself for it, for I know your anxiety. I am very well. My affairs are moving prosperously. I am in a miserable village, where I must still remain for some time. Tin's is not like being in a great city. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Osterode: reproaching himself for silence.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — I congratulate you on the confinement of the princess; I am very anxious to learn that she is doing well and out of all danger. I hope that your daughter will be as good and as amiable as her mother. It remains for you now to have a boy next year. Have your daughter called Josephine. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Italy held while Poland bleeds.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" Napoleon," The lady in question, who had played the part of the Goddess of Reason during the orgies of the Revolution, in 1807 was representing "Glory" at the Opera, when she fell and broke her arm. The Empress was present when the accident occurred, and was much shocked. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Fouche from Osterode, 1807-03-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I learn, my love, that the mischievous talk which was held in your saloon, at Mayence, is renewed. Silence it. I shall be much displeased if you do not find a remedy for this. You allow yourself to be afflicted by the remarks of those who ought to comfort you. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Silence the Mayence salon gossip.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have seen in the newspapers a pretended letter written in Russia. It is lamentable. We do not require to be defended by fables. No man in his senses will be deceived, and it will only create a bad effect. The Russians belonging to the army never say among themselves that they gained the battle. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Conspiracies watched.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is not right for you to go with humble equipage to the minor theaters. That is not suitable to your rank. You ought only to go to the large theaters in impsoing state. Live as you were accustomed to do when I was in Paris. My health is very good. The weather has changed to cold. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Humble equipage unworthy of her rank (×2 letters).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “There can be no doubt that Rear-Admiral Allemand should not attack an equal force of the enemy, much more a superior force. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: The navy ordered from a Polish mill town.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Did I ever give you an order to send 10,000 Prussians to Spain 1 I told my Minister for Foreign Affairs to make such a proposal to Spain, but was that equivalent to an an order from me.'' This sort of thing has happened. several times. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: War administration.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am delighted to hear nothing more of Madame de Stael. When I trouble myself about her it is when I have facts before me. That woman is a regular crow; she thought that she saw the tempest coming. Let her go to her Lake Leman. " NAPOLEON." To M. CAMBACERS. " FiNKENSTEIN, iqtk April, 1807. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Police before the spring campaign.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “England and Sweden adhered to this convention, and the former promised to send 20,000 men to the Baltic to operate against the French flank and rear. A separate agreement was concluded between Prussia and England; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Fouche from P'Inkenstein, 1807-04-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I write you a word. I have removed ray headquarters to a very pleasant chateau, something like that of Bessieres, where I have many fire-places. This is very grateful to me, as I rise often in the night. I love to see the fire. My health is perfect. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Finckenstein: pleasant château like Bessieres'.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — Send General Lauriston twenty-five gold and silver watches to be given to the Turks. Also send twenty-five to Marmont. " Napoleon." to the king of holland. " FiNKENSTEiisr, ii,tk April, 1807. "You say that you have 20,000 men with the grand army. You do not believe this yourself. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Italy governed from a Polish château.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “"You say that you have 20,000 men with the grand army. You do not believe this yourself. You have only 10,000; and what men! You should make soldiers instead of marshals, knights, and counts. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Prince Eugene from Finkenstein, 1807-04-04. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I must say that I was not pleased with the preamble of your order for suppressing the monasteries. With regard to all that concerns religion you must use the language of religion, and not that of philosophy. That is the great art of the person who governs. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, FlNKENSTElN, 1807-04-14
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Joseph's kingdom supervised.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" No matter what pleasure it gives me to interest myself in all that concerns the welfare of my people, it would be going too far to mix myself up in theatrical squabbles. I therefore give you the exclusive supervision of the opera until my return. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Naples, FlNKENSTElN, 1807-04-14
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The King Of Naples from Flnkensteln, 1807-04-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “1 have your letter of the 5th of April. I see with pain that you are chagrined at what I said to you. As usual, your little Creole head becomes excited and afflicted, " tu petite tete Creole se monte et s'afflige" Let us then say no more about it. I am very well. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Her little Creole temper; chagrin read with pain.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The aides-de-camp of Marshal Angereau, instead of remaining with the army, have followed him to Paris. Let me know to what corps they belong, for it is not my intention to allow them to remain in Paris. "Napoleon." They might say more than was agreeable about Eylau.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Spring campaign prepared.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It seems to me that I wrote to the Princess Pauline that she might go to the waters. I only opposed this by way of advice, because I see that the doctors order waters when they want to get rid of their patients. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Paris briefed for Friedland.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I see with pleasure that you are in good health, and that you are always fond of the Malmaison. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Finkenstein, 1807-05-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter. I do not understand what you tell me about ladies in correspondence with me. I love none but my little Josephine, good, pouting, and capricious, who knows how to quarrel with grace, as she does every thing else; […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: No ladies in correspondence with me.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 2d of May, in which I see that you are inclined to go to St. Cloud. I have seen with pain the bad conduct of Madame. Could you not speak to her to amend her life? Such conduct must soon draw upon her serious disagreements with her husband. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: St. Cloud instead? Seen with pain.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I can appreciate the grief which the death of poor Napoleon has caused you. You can understand the anguish which I experience. I could wish that I were with you, that you might become moderate and discreet in your grief. You have had the happiness of never losing any children. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Poor Napoleon's death grieved them (nephew).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 6th of May. I see in it already the injury which you are suffering; and I fear that you are not reasonable, and that you afflict yourself too much from the calamity which has befallen us. Adieu, my love. Entirely thine. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Hortense arrived; injury already suffered.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 10th of May. I see that you have gone to Lucken. I think that you may rest there a fortnight. That will give much pleasure to the Belgians, and will serve to divert your mind. I see with pain that you are not wise. Grief has bounds which it should not pass. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Lucken rest a fortnight.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 16th, and see with pleasure that Hortense has arrived at Lucken. I am, indeed, grieved by what you tell me of the state of stupor in which she still continues. She should have more fortitude and should govern herself. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Hortense at Lucken; grieved.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Russian army was more crushed and beaten than ever the Austrians were. (?) Beningsen, who commanded them, displayed very little talent. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Cambaceres from Tilsit, 1807-06-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I have just seen the Emperor Alexander; I was well satisfied with him; he is a handsome, good, and youthful Emperor; he has more intelligence than is generally supposed. He is coming to stay at Tilsit to-morrow. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Friedland eve from Tilsit.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “\ " I have just seen the Emperor of Russia in the middle of the Niemen on a raft where a handsome flag was hoisted. To-morrow the Emperor is going to present the King of Prussia to me, and is coming to reside here. To that effect I have neutralised the town ofTilsit. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Diplomacy ready for victory.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “treaty as published by order of the Cortes in 18 12, being inclined to believe, from what afterwards happened, that it is in conformity with what was really agreed upon between Napoleon and Alexander. The articles ran thus: — ■ Art. I. Russia […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. De Talleyrand from Tilsit, 1807-06-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am very well, my love. Your letter of yesterday gave me much pain. It appears that you are continually sad and that you are not reasonable. The weather is very bad. Adieu, my love; I love you and desire to hear that are cheerful and contented. NAPOLEON.”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Continually sad; giving pain.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The whole Russian army routed, 80 guns captured, 30,000 men taken prisoners or killed, with twenty-five generals; the Russian guard annihilated; it is the worthy sister of Marengo, Austerlitz, and Jena. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from 15M, 1807-06-15. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “While waiting for St. Denis to be ready,- have the body of the little Napoleon placed in a chapel at Notre Dame. On the same day, in a Proclamation to the army, the Emperor said — " Frenchmen, you are worthy of yourselves and of me. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Friedland won: Paris told first.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “1 The remains of the "little Napoleon" were in due time transferred to St. Denis, but Louis XVIII. had them afterwards removed from that burial place of the French kings. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Cambaceris from Tilsit, 1807-06-22. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Friedland fune 24, i8oy. " Soldiers: On the 5th of June we were attacked in our cantonments by the Russian army. The enemy had mistaken the cause of our inactivity. He perceived too late that our repose was that of a lion. He repents of having disturbed it. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Friedland victory proclaimed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Let me know if there are any muskets'at Koenigsberg. I was told that there were 160,000, and since then I hear nothing more about them. As I have announced this fact everywhere, I shall be very angry if I have been deceived. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Niemen raft politics: emperors meet.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I have just come from an interview with the Emperor Alexander. He is a very handsome, amiable, and youthful emperor. He has more ability than is generally supposed. To-morrow he takes his lodgings in the city of Tilsit. Adieu, my love. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Tilsit: just met Emperor Alexander — handsome, amiable, youthful.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I had to defend myself against being obliged to make some further concessions to her husband; I was galant, but adhered to my policy. The Queen is very amiable. When you read this letter peace will have been concluded with Russia and Prussia, and Jerome recognised as King of Westphalia.,. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Tilsit, 1807-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “she is full of coquetterie towards me. But do not be jealous; I am an oilcloth off which all that runs. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Tilsit, 1807-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Peace has been signed and ratified, 1 Poor Selim had been dethroned, and his nephew, Mustapha, now ruled in his stead. and everything is going on well. That arch madman, the King of Sweden, has seized this opportunity to denounce the armistice. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. De Talleyrand from Tilsit, 1807-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “an army of 20,000 Frenchmen will march to Bayonne on the ist September to join a Spanish army and to conquer Portugal. In a despatch of the 16th October, Prince Metternich gives a description of the violent language addressed to various ambassadors. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. De Talleyrand from Dresden, 1807-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain). Trivial OCR repair.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with pain that you are an egotist, and that the success of my arms has no attraction for you. "The handsome Queen of Prussia is to come to dine with me to-day. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Empress from Tilsit, 1807-07-06. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother, — Desirous of placing near your Majesty some one who will be able to express to you viva voce the sentiments with which you have inspired me, I send you my aide-de-camp, the General of Division, Savary, whom I have appointed ambassador to your court. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Emperor of Russia, KCENIGSBERG, 1807-07-14
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: New ally flattered after Tilsit.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg your Majesty to receive him with that kindness which is peculiar to you. Savary, who must have reminded the Czar painfully of Austerlitz and of the violent death of the Due d'Enghien. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Emperor Of Russia, KCENIGSBERG, 1807-07-14
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Emperor Of Russia from Kcenigsberg, 1807-07-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love — I arrived yesterday, at five o'clock in the evening, at Dresden, in very good health, although I have been a hundred hours in the carriage without leaving it. I am here at the house of the King of Saxony, with whom I am very much pleased. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Printed 1801 in error; Dresden stay was July 1807 on the Tilsit return.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write to M. Alquier to present a note in which he will insist on the number of French cardinals being Vide thirty-fourth bulletin. " The Russians ill-treat the poor as well as the rich. They plunder, burn villages, and massacre— these are their amusements. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Return journey diplomacy.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall not fear to assemble the Galilean, Italian, German, and Polish Churches in council to do my work without a Pope, and to protect my people against the pretensions of the prie […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. De Talleyrand from Dresden, 1807-07-22. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If England refuses to accept the Russian mediation, Denmark must declare war against her, or I must declare war against Denmark. In the latter case your duty will be to seize on the whole Danish continent. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Hanseatic governance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I do not know what rash act you suppose the Pope to be capable of committing. You should have sent some troops in the direction of Bologna, and if he commits an imprudence it will be a fine opportunity for depriving him of the Roman States. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Italy after Tilsit.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In spite of his ardent desire to be agreeable to his Majesty he could not render himself guilty of an abominable abuse before the throne of the Almighty. That Napoleon had some reason to complain that the objections raised by the Pope we […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Prince Eugene from 4M, 1807-08-04. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am proprietor, in the duchy of Warsaw, of all the debts due to the King of Prussia by private individuals. These debts are due for money advanced to proprietors on the security of their land. They appear to amount to a sum of 60,000,000 francs. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

displayText: “Which is the best port for assembling my squadron of the ocean? I see only two between which to choose — Brest or Cherbourg. Which of those two ports offers the greatest facilities for invading England or Ireland? Which of the two offers the greatest facilities for sailing to America and India?. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: The navy in the northern scheme.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg that you will have the fortifications of Geneva blown up. Perhaps in a military point of view it would be of interest to keep this place; but, the inhabitants having always exhibited a bad feeling, I have decided upon blowing up the fortifications without delay. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: War ministry builds the invasion.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Boulogne flotilla has returned to harbour. It sustained some damage. I think even that a gunboat went down. Write that this should cause no discouragement. These gales are just the things to exercise the crews. " Napoleon.'* To marshal berthier. "St. Cloud, 13rd August, 1811. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Baltic combinations.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" Express my displeasure to Marshal Soult for sending me the flags of Albuera by a foreigner. It appears that he was in the Austrian service, and he must therefore have fought against us. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter concerning the cheating of Bourrienne at Hamburg. It will be important to throw light upon what he has done. Have the Jew, Gumprecht Mares, arrested, seize his papers, and place him in solitary confinement. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg that you will pay 2,500 francs a month to the ex-Queen of Etruria, at her convent in Rome. The poor Queen of Etruria, deprived of her kingdom, which was handed over by Napoleon to his sister Eliza, was most cruelly treated. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: Treasury for 600,000 men.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" I have sent a courier to Berlin to-day to tell Comte St. Marsau to leave that capital if the Prussians continue their fortifications and provisioning Spandau and Kolberg. […]”

displayText: “As for the 1 Nearly all the Bonapartes flocked thither after Waterloo. King [poor Louis] they remember him only as a good sort of man, very changeable, who had very limited views on the subject of administration, and who undid in the evening what he had done in the morning. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They must give as a reason the Russian levy of four men in every 500, the large number of troops on the frontier, and the decision at which Russia seems to have arrived of making war. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just seen the porcelain service sent to the Empress as a new year's gift. It is very ugly. See that it be prettier another year. Have a breakfast service made, and on each cup the portraits of the Empress and of the six princesses, my sisters and sister-in-law. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vol. III — public domain
context: New Year's diplomacy.
